Quantization error accumulation anisotropy refers to the empirical observation that quantization noise does not distribute uniformly across a transformer's depth: early layers, attention output projections, and certain MLP gate activations in gated-linear-unit architectures accumulate disproportionately large representational distortion relative to their nominal bit-width budget, while other layers tolerate aggressive quantization with near-zero degradation. The central question is whether this depth-dependent sensitivity profile is structurally determined — by weight matrix condition number, activation kurtosis, or gradient flow geometry — or whether it emerges dynamically from the interaction between per-channel calibration statistics and the specific mixed-precision assignment policy. Per-channel asymmetric calibration (distinct scale and zero-point per output channel) is meant to tighten the clipping range to the actual distribution of each channel, but when channels within the same layer exhibit wildly different kurtosis (common in post-LayerNorm activations), the per-channel granularity still under-fits the true distribution tail, and the resulting clipping error is absorbed downstream by whatever layer receives those activations — creating non-local error propagation that static calibration cannot observe. The expert worry that beginners miss is that INT8 calibration metrics like SQNR or mean absolute error on held-out calibration data are measured layer-locally, so a layer that looks quantization-tolerant in isolation can silently become a catastrophic error amplifier once upstream layers are simultaneously quantized and their distorted outputs land in its weight-activation product — this compositional failure mode is invisible to per-layer sensitivity analysis and only surfaces in end-to-end perplexity or task evaluation. Compounding this, mixed-precision schedulers that assign 4-bit to "low-sensitivity" layers based on single-layer Hessian traces systematically underestimate cross-layer error compounding because the Hessian is computed with full-precision activations, not the quantized activations that will actually flow at inference time.

When calibration corpus activations underrepresent the true deployment distribution's tail — a near-universal condition for high-kurtosis channels in post-LayerNorm projections, where LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., 2022) documented outlier magnitudes 100× the median channel magnitude — the calibrated clipping boundary is set too tight, and all deployment activations exceeding that boundary are clipped to the same maximum quantized value, converting what should be a variance-preserving rounding error into a one-sided truncation bias. This bias is systematic rather than random because the outlier channels in transformer hidden states are structurally stable: Kovaleva et al. and subsequent mechanistic work show that specific head output channels persistently carry high-magnitude signals tied to attention sink tokens and positional encoding residuals, meaning the miscalibration hits the same semantic subspace on every forward pass rather than diffusing across the representation. Under asymmetric INT8, the zero-point q_z = round(−x_min · s⁻¹) is estimated from calibration x_min, but if deployment x_min is more negative (as happens with kurtotic channels whose negative tail the calibration corpus undersampled), the stored zero-point is systematically too high, shifting the entire quantized range upward and producing a negative bias on all reconstructed activations in that channel — not just the clipped ones. SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) quantifies this as a per-channel "migration difficulty" and shows that for channels with calibration-to-deployment distribution shift, the effective zero-point error alone can account for 0.3–0.8 perplexity points on Wikitext-103 before any rounding error is added. The asymmetry implies a directional degradation: downstream layers receive activations that are biased low in precisely those channels that carry the highest-magnitude semantic content, and because these channels dominate the weight-activation inner product in subsequent projections, the bias is amplified rather than averaged out — the opposite of what you'd hope from the law of large numbers across channels.

The post-hoc LoRA correction framing is theoretically sound and has a direct empirical ancestor in LoftQ (Liu et al., 2023), which initializes LoRA adapters specifically to absorb the residual between full-precision and quantized weights via alternating SVD — demonstrating that rank-8 to rank-16 corrections recover most quantization-induced perplexity degradation on LLaMA-2-7B within ~1% of fp16 baseline, suggesting the perturbation is indeed low-rank enough to be captured this way. The detection problem is harder than the correction problem: to isolate the α-miscalibration component of the perturbation from ordinary quantization rounding noise, you need activation statistics from the deployment distribution to reconstruct what s_j should have been, then compute ΔW̃_j = W_j(s_j^{calib} − s_j^{deploy}) per channel and take its SVD — but this requires either online activation collection or a proxy deployment corpus, and the rank-r truncation is only stable if the top-r singular values of ΔW̃ are well-separated from the noise floor set by rounding error, which empirically holds for r ≤ 4 in most MLP projections but degrades for attention Q/K projections where weight spectra are flatter. For token count, QuIP# (Tseng et al., 2024) and related quantization-aware fine-tuning work suggest a phase transition around 128–512 tokens per layer for estimating a rank-4 correction: below ~128 tokens the activation covariance estimate is too noisy for the cross-term ΔW̃·ΔX̃ to be reliably decomposed, while above ~512 tokens diminishing returns set in because the low-rank subspace is already well-characterized and additional tokens primarily refine the noise floor rather than the signal subspace. Re-running SmoothQuant with a better corpus is cheaper in compute but strictly worse in expressivity: it can only adjust the scalar s_j per channel and cannot correct for the fact that α miscalibration produces a perturbation with off-diagonal channel interactions when outlier channels co-activate — a rank-r LoRA correction with r ≥ 2 can absorb these cross-channel terms while re-calibration cannot. The practical recommendation emerging from this analysis is a two-stage pipeline: re-calibrate α with ~256 deployment-domain tokens to fix the dominant diagonal miscalibration, then apply a rank-2 LoRA correction estimated from the same tokens to absorb residual cross-channel structured error — this combination outperforms either intervention alone at a total cost of roughly 0.1% of the original pretraining compute for a 7B model.

When A and B are quantized independently to INT8, the reconstructed adapter BA introduces a perturbation ΔBA = ΔB·A + B·ΔA + ΔB·ΔA whose Frobenius norm scales as O(r · ε · σ_max) where ε is the per-element quantization step and σ_max is the largest singular value of the adapter — critically, because BA is rank-r by construction, its quantization error is not rank-r but full-rank, meaning the correction intended to suppress a structured rank-r perturbation re-introduces unstructured full-rank noise that cannot be further compressed without another correction layer. LoftQ's empirical results hint at this: their alternating quantization-SVD procedure requires 5–10 iterations to stabilize, and the per-iteration perplexity improvement follows a geometric decay with ratio ~0.3–0.5, suggesting convergence but also that each quantize-correct cycle recovers only a fraction of the previous cycle's residual rather than fully canceling it. The fixed-point stability condition can be stated precisely: the iterative scheme W_{n+1} = Q(W_0 + B_n A_n) with B_{n+1}A_{n+1} = SVD_r(W_0 − W_{n+1}) converges if and only if the spectral norm of the quantization operator's Jacobian restricted to the rank-r subspace is less than 1, which in practice requires that the quantization step ε be small enough that round-trip error ‖Q(BA) − BA‖ < ‖W_0 − Q(W_0)‖ — satisfied for INT8 adapter quantization when σ_max(BA) is kept below ~0.1·σ_max(W_0) by regularizing adapter initialization. QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) sidesteps this instability by keeping adapters in BF16 while only quantizing the base weight, effectively decoupling the two quantization grids — but this is only viable when adapter storage cost is acceptable, and in extremely memory-constrained deployments where adapters must also be INT4, the cross-term ΔB·ΔA becomes the dominant error source and the fixed-point may not exist for r > 2 under INT4. The deepest instability is that the SVD truncation in each correction step is computed on the quantized residual, not the true residual, so truncation error and quantization error compound multiplicatively across iterations rather than additively — this is why empirical practitioners cap iterative LoftQ at 5 iterations regardless of convergence criteria, since beyond that the noise floor of the quantized SVD exceeds the signal being corrected.

On H100 and A100 GPUs, INT4 weight quantization delivers its throughput benefit almost entirely through memory bandwidth reduction during weight loading — a 4× reduction in bytes moved from HBM — rather than through tensor core arithmetic speedup, since NVIDIA tensor cores natively support INT8 and BF16 but require INT4 weights to be unpacked to INT8 before GEMM execution via inline dequantization in the CUDA kernel (as implemented in CUTLASS and the Marlin kernel by Frantar & Alistarh, 2024). The BF16 adapter addition BA + W_dequant must occur after dequantization, meaning the effective memory access pattern is: load INT4 W_q (narrow), load BF16 A and B (wide), dequantize W_q to BF16, compute BA in BF16, add — and this serialized sequence breaks the fused dequantize-GEMM kernel that makes INT4 fast in the first place, because standard INT4 kernels like Marlin fuse dequantization directly into the tensor core accumulation loop and cannot accommodate an additive BF16 term mid-pipeline without a separate kernel launch. Memory coalescing is the concrete bottleneck: INT4 weights pack two values per byte and are laid out for 128-byte cache line reads optimized for the dequantization warp schedule, while BF16 adapter matrices have a completely different access pattern optimized for tensor core tile sizes (typically 16×16×16 or 16×16×8 on H100), so loading both in the same kernel either wastes L2 cache capacity through dtype-misaligned accesses or requires double-buffering that partially negates the HBM bandwidth savings. Empirically, the Marlin kernel achieves ~3.6× throughput over BF16 for pure INT4 weight-only quantization on A100 at batch size 1, but adding a BF16 LoRA adapter via a separate GEMM and elementwise add (as in the reference QLoRA inference path) reduces the effective speedup to ~1.8–2.1× in practice, measured in tokens/second on LLaMA-2-7B — roughly half the theoretical gain lost to the dtype boundary overhead. The latency penalty is batch-size dependent in a critical way: at batch size 1 (decode-dominated inference), memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and the penalty is severe; at batch size ≥ 32 (prefill or throughput-oriented serving), compute becomes the bottleneck and the relative cost of the BF16 adapter addition shrinks because BA can be precomputed and merged into W before batched requests arrive — which is why production systems like vLLM with LoRA support offer a "merge-and-unload" mode that folds BA into W_dequant at serving time, accepting a one-time dequantization cost to eliminate the per-forward-pass dtype boundary entirely.

The most non-obvious fact is that quantization error anisotropy across transformer depth is not monotonically increasing with depth — it exhibits a bimodal accumulation profile with a secondary peak at the final 10–15% of layers that is mechanistically distinct from the early-layer peak. The early-layer sensitivity is well-documented and tied to embedding space geometry: layers 0–4 in LLaMA-class models handle token identity information in a nearly one-hot subspace where small quantization errors cause disproportionate semantic confusion. But the late-layer peak, documented in ZeroQuant-V2 (Yao et al., 2023) and reproduced in SpQR (Dettmers et al., 2023) sensitivity analyses, arises from a different mechanism: the final layers must compress the full residual stream into a vocabulary-sized logit distribution via the unembedding matrix, and because the unembedding projection amplifies differences in the last hidden state by a factor proportional to the condition number of the unembedding matrix (often 10³–10⁴ for 32K+ vocabulary models), quantization noise in layers N-5 through N is amplified into logit space far more aggressively than noise in mid-network layers. This means mixed-precision schedulers that assign bit-width based on a smooth depth-indexed sensitivity curve — a common heuristic — systematically under-protect the final layer cluster while wasting bits on mid-network layers that could tolerate INT4, and the perplexity cost of this misallocation is concentrated in low-probability token predictions (the tail of the softmax) rather than top-1 accuracy, making it invisible to accuracy-based evaluation but catastrophic for log-likelihood-based metrics and sampling diversity.

Weight tying creates a genuinely pathological quantization coupling that is absent in untied architectures: the same INT4 or INT8 quantized tensor E serves as both the input lookup table (where each token retrieval selects one row, so quantization error affects only the selected row's embedding vector) and the unembedding projection (where the full matrix multiplies the final hidden state, so quantization error in every row contributes to every logit simultaneously). This asymmetry in how the same quantization error manifests — sparse row-wise at input, dense matrix-wise at output — means the effective quantization noise seen by the vocabulary projection is O(V) times larger in expectation than the noise seen by any single token embedding, where V is vocabulary size; for a 32K vocabulary model this is a ~32,000× difference in error exposure between the two uses of the same weight tensor. GPT-2 (which uses weight tying) exhibits this concretely: GPTQ applied to GPT-2-XL shows that quantizing the tied embedding matrix to INT4 degrades perplexity by 1.8–2.3 points more than quantizing an equivalent untied unembedding matrix in LLaMA-class models at the same bit-width, a gap attributable specifically to the dense unembedding use case rather than the embedding lookup. The anisotropy profile in tied models therefore collapses the bimodal early/late structure into a single dominant sensitivity spike at the shared weight: per-channel calibration for the unembedding use case (which needs tight per-output-channel scales over the full hidden dimension) is fundamentally incompatible with per-channel calibration for the embedding use case (which needs per-token-type scales over vocabulary rows), and any single calibration granularity is a compromise that sub-optimally serves both. Practical quantization toolkits like bitsandbytes and AutoGPTQ handle this by either forcing the tied weight to full precision (a significant memory cost for large vocabularies) or applying separate fake-quantization passes for each use case and averaging the resulting scales — the latter producing a hybrid scale that is provably suboptimal for both uses but empirically loses only 0.3–0.6 perplexity points versus full-precision on WikiText-103, suggesting the two calibration objectives are not maximally adversarial in practice.
